chapters.n: Mormon, the prophet-historian who abridged most of the Book of Mormon, now writes his own eyewitness account. This smaller book within the larger record bears his name.

f.g: Here the short book Mormon wrote about his own times, not the whole volume.

chapters.n: Around the time Ammaron hid the records, he approached Mormon, about ten years old and receiving some education. Ammaron saw that he was a “sober” child — serious and thoughtful — and observant.
Ammaron tells Mormon to remember what he observes, and at about age 24 to go to the hill Shim in the land Antum, where the sacred records are deposited.

f.w: a hill which shall be called Shim
f.g: A hill in the land northward; distinct from the hill Cumorah.

chapters.n: He is to take only the plates of Nephi, leave the rest, and record on them what he observes about the people.

f.g: The large plates, the ongoing historical record.

chapters.n: Mormon is a descendant of Nephi, and his father was also named Mormon. He remembers Ammaron’s charge.

f.g: The name Mormon recalls the waters of Mormon where Alma baptized (Mosiah 18:4).

chapters.n: At eleven, Mormon’s father takes him south to the land of Zarahemla, the old Nephite heartland.
Mormon is struck by how built-up and crowded the land has become — people almost as numerous as sand on the seashore.
That year war breaks out between the Nephites (with Jacobites, Josephites, and Zoramites) and the Lamanites (with Lemuelites and Ishmaelites). The old tribal divisions are now battle lines.

f.w: Jacobites and the Josephites and the Zoramites

chapters.n: For simplicity, the sides are called Nephites and Lamanites.
The war begins at the borders of Zarahemla near the river Sidon, the major river of Nephite lands.
The Nephites gather over 30,000 men and win several battles that year.
The Lamanites give up their plans, and peace lasts about four years with no bloodshed.
But wickedness spreads everywhere, so the Lord takes away his beloved disciples, and miracles and healings stop because of the people’s sin.

f.w: the Lord did take away his beloved disciples
f.g: The Three Nephites ceased ministering openly among them.

chapters.n: Spiritual gifts disappear and the Holy Ghost comes upon no one, because of wickedness and unbelief.

f.w: there were no gifts from the Lord

chapters.n: At fifteen, Mormon, “somewhat of a sober mind,” is visited by the Lord and personally tastes the goodness of Jesus. In a dark age, one young man finds deep faith.

f.w: tasted and knew of the goodness of Jesus

chapters.n: Mormon tries to preach, but his mouth is shut and he is forbidden, because the people have willfully rebelled against God.
He stays among them but may not preach because of their hard hearts, and the land is cursed for their sake.
Gadianton robbers infest the land. People bury their treasures, but they become “slippery” — they cannot keep hold of them — fulfilling Samuel the Lamanite’s prophecy.

f.g: Lost or slipping away so they could not be kept.

chapters.n: Sorcery, witchcraft, and magic abound, and the devil’s power is felt everywhere, fulfilling the warnings of Abinadi and Samuel.
War returns that same year. Although Mormon is young, he is physically big, so the Nephites make him leader of their armies.
At age sixteen Mormon leads a Nephite army against the Lamanites, in the year 326 after Christ’s sign.

f.g: Compare Helaman’s young warriors and Moroni, who led at 25 (Alma 43:17).

chapters.n: In 327 the Lamanites attack in such force that Mormon’s armies are terrified, refuse to fight, and retreat north.
They take the city of Angola and fortify it with all their strength, but the Lamanites still drive them out.

f.g: Strengthen defenses with walls and earthworks.

chapters.n: They are also driven out of the land of David.
They march to the land of Joshua, near the western seashore.
Mormon gathers the people as quickly as possible into one body for protection — a strategy he will repeat.
Robbers and Lamanites fill the land. Even with destruction hanging over them, the Nephites do not repent, and bloodshed spreads everywhere — the whole land is in upheaval.
The Lamanite king Aaron comes with 44,000 men; Mormon meets him with 42,000 and drives him back. It is now 330 years after Christ.
The Nephites start to cry out and seem to repent, as Samuel had prophesied, because no one can keep his possessions with thieves, robbers, murderers, and magic everywhere.

f.w: as had been prophesied by Samuel

chapters.n: Mourning and lamentation spread throughout the land, especially among the Nephites.
Seeing their sorrow, Mormon rejoices, hoping the Lord in his mercy and patience will help them become righteous again.
But his joy is short-lived: their sorrow is not godly sorrow that leads to repentance. It is the “sorrowing of the damned” — regret at the pain of sin, not a desire to change.

f.w: suffer them to take happiness in sin

chapters.n: They do not come to Jesus with broken hearts and contrite spirits. Instead they curse God and wish to die — yet still fight with the sword to stay alive.
Mormon’s sorrow returns. He sees that their “day of grace” has passed — their opportunity has closed — as thousands die in open rebellion. It is now 344 years after Christ.

f.w: the day of grace was passed

f.g: Left unburied like refuse — a sign of utter disgrace.

chapters.n: In 345 the Nephites flee before the Lamanites until they reach the land of Jashon.

f.g: A land in the north near the hill Shim.

chapters.n: Jashon is near where Ammaron hid the records. Mormon has followed Ammaron’s instructions, taken the plates of Nephi, and begun his record.

f.w: according to the word of Ammaron

chapters.n: On the large plates of Nephi Mormon wrote a full account of the people’s wickedness, but on these plates he holds back. He has witnessed wickedness his whole life.

f.g: The plates of Mormon, his abridged record.

chapters.n: Mormon mourns that he has been filled with sorrow all his days, yet he knows he will be lifted up at the last day. Hope survives in his personal faith.

f.w: lifted up at the last day

chapters.n: That year the Nephites are hunted again and driven north to the land of Shem.
They fortify the city of Shem and gather in as many people as possible, hoping to save them.
In 346 the Lamanites attack again.
Mormon passionately urges the people to stand boldly and fight for their wives, children, and homes — echoing Captain Moroni’s title of liberty.

f.w: fight for their wives, and their children

chapters.n: His words rouse them somewhat, and they stand firm rather than flee.
With 30,000 men they hold off 50,000 Lamanites so firmly that the Lamanites flee.
They pursue and defeat the Lamanites again, but Mormon notes the Lord’s strength is not with them. Left to themselves without the Spirit, they are no stronger than their enemies.
Mormon grieves over this calamity caused by wickedness. Still, they fight on against Lamanites and Gadianton robbers until they regain their lands.
In 350 the Nephites make a treaty with the Lamanites and the Gadianton robbers, dividing the lands of inheritance.
The Nephites receive the land northward up to the narrow passage, and the Lamanites receive all the land southward. The once-united land is now formally split.

f.g: Connected to the narrow neck of land.

chapters.n: Ten years of peace follow the treaty. Mormon uses the time to have the Nephites prepare their lands and weapons for the next war.
The Lord tells Mormon to call the people to repent, be baptized, and rebuild his church — and they will be spared. Even now, God offers a way out.
Mormon preaches, but in vain. The people do not realize it was the Lord who had spared them and given them a chance to repent; they harden their hearts.
At the end of the ten years (360 years after Christ), the Lamanite king sends Mormon a letter announcing they are preparing to attack again.
Mormon gathers his people to the land Desolation, at a border city near the narrow pass to the south.

f.g: Named for the ruins of the Jaredite civilization found there.

chapters.n: They station their armies there to block the Lamanites and fortify with all their strength.
In 361 the Lamanites attack the city of Desolation and are beaten back to their own lands.
In 362 they attack again, and the Nephites win again, killing many; the dead are thrown into the sea.
These victories make the Nephites boast in their own strength and swear before heaven to take revenge for their slain kin.
They swear by heaven and even by God’s throne to go on the offensive and wipe out their enemies — something Christ had forbidden.
Mormon completely refuses to lead them any longer because of their wickedness. This is a defining moment of moral courage.
He had led them many times despite their wickedness, loved them with God’s love, and prayed for them all day long — but without faith that anything would change, because their hearts were so hard.

f.w: according to the love of God which was in me

chapters.n: Three times he delivered them from their enemies, and still they did not repent.
When they swore by everything Christ forbade to go up and take revenge, the Lord spoke to Mormon.
“Vengeance is mine, and I will repay.” Because they did not repent after being delivered, they will be destroyed. Revenge belongs to God, not to people.

f.w: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay
cut off from the face of the earth

chapters.n: Mormon obeys and refuses to go to battle. He stands as an “idle witness” — a bystander who observes and records — to show the world what he saw, guided by the Spirit.

f.g: A witness who takes no part in the action but records it.

chapters.n: So Mormon writes to the latter-day Gentiles and to Israel, for the time when Israel prepares to return to its lands of inheritance.
He writes to the whole world and to the twelve tribes of Israel, who will be judged by the twelve apostles Jesus chose in Jerusalem.

f.w: the twelve whom Jesus chose to be his disciples

chapters.n: He also writes to the remnant of his own people, who will be judged by the Nephite twelve, who in turn answer to the twelve in Jerusalem. Judgment is ordered and fair.

f.w: the twelve whom Jesus chose in this land

chapters.n: The Spirit shows him that all humanity, every descendant of Adam, must stand before Christ’s judgment seat to be judged by their works.

He writes so people will believe the gospel they will have among them, and so the Jews will have another witness that Jesus, whom they crucified, is the very Christ and very God — a key purpose of the Book of Mormon.

f.w: the very Christ and the very God

chapters.n: Mormon wishes he could persuade the whole earth to repent and prepare for Christ’s judgment. His heart reaches across the centuries to us.
In 363 the Nephites do what Mormon refused to lead: they march out of Desolation to attack the Lamanites first.

f.w: did go up with their armies

chapters.n: They are driven back to Desolation, and while exhausted, a fresh Lamanite army strikes. The Lamanites capture the city, kill many Nephites, and take many prisoners.
Survivors flee to the city of Teancum, on the seashore near Desolation.

f.g: Probably named for the famous Nephite captain Teancum.

chapters.n: Mormon explains why: they lost because they went on the attack. Had they stayed defensive, the Lamanites would have had no power over them.
A key principle: God’s judgments overtake the wicked, often by means of other wicked people. It is the wicked who stir up hearts to violence.

f.w: it is by the wicked that the wicked are punished

chapters.n: The Lamanites prepare to attack Teancum.
In 364 the Lamanites come against Teancum to capture it too.
The Nephites drive them back — and immediately boast in their own strength again, then march out and retake Desolation.
By now thousands have died on both sides.
In 366 the Lamanites attack again. The Nephites still do not repent and continue in constant wickedness.
Mormon says no tongue or pen can describe the horror of the bloodshed. Every heart is hardened, and people actually delight in shedding blood.

f.w: delighted in the shedding of blood

chapters.n: There had never been such great wickedness among Lehi’s descendants, or even in all of Israel. It is a staggering statement from someone who knew Israel’s history.

f.w: according to the words of the Lord

chapters.n: Outnumbered, the Nephites lose Desolation to the Lamanites.
The Lamanites drive the people out of Teancum, capture many women and children, and offer them as human sacrifices to their idols.
In 367 the Nephites, enraged by these sacrifices, attack in great anger and drive the Lamanites out of their lands. Anger, not faith, now drives them.

f.g: Compare Moroni 9:3-5 on the Nephites being without restraint.

chapters.n: The Lamanites do not return until 375.
Then they come with all their forces, too many to count.
From then on the Nephites never again prevail; they are swept away like dew before the sun — quickly and completely.

f.w: as a dew before the sun

chapters.n: The Lamanites attack Desolation in a fierce battle and defeat the Nephites.
The Nephites flee to the city of Boaz and fight so boldly that the Lamanites cannot take it until a second assault.
On the second attack the Nephites are slaughtered, and their women and children are again sacrificed to idols.
The Nephites flee again, taking all the inhabitants of the towns and villages with them.
Seeing the land about to fall, Mormon goes to the hill Shim and takes all the records Ammaron had hidden, to keep them safe.

f.w: did take up all the records

chapters.n: Mormon repents of his oath never to help the Nephites again and takes command of their armies once more. They look to him as a deliverer, though he knows better.
Mormon has no hope for them, knowing God’s judgments are coming. They fight to survive but never call on the God who made them.
The Lamanites attack the Nephites at the city of Jordan but are driven back for the time being.
They come again, but the Nephites hold Jordan and other strongholds, blocking the Lamanites from the land beyond.
But every land the Nephites passed without gathering its people was destroyed, and its towns burned. It is now 379 years after Christ.
In 380 the Lamanites come again. The Nephites stand boldly, but the Lamanites are so numerous they trample them.

f.w: tread the people of the Nephites under their feet

chapters.n: The Nephites flee. Those faster than the Lamanites escape; the slower are cut down.
Mormon does not want to “harrow up” readers’ souls with such horrors, but knows these things must be made known — all hidden things will be proclaimed from the housetops.

f.g: Tear up or deeply distress, like a harrow breaking up soil.

chapters.n: He writes only a brief abridgment, partly by commandment and partly to spare readers excessive sorrow. The knowledge must reach the remnant and the Gentiles who will scatter them.
He speaks to the descendants of these people and to the Gentiles who care for Israel and know the source of their blessings.
Such readers will grieve over Israel’s calamity and that these people did not repent and let Jesus embrace them.

f.w: clasped in the arms of Jesus

chapters.n: This record is written for the remnant of Jacob. Since their wickedness will prevent them from bringing it forth, it will be hidden and come forth in God’s time.
Mormon has been commanded so: the record will come forth when the Lord sees fit.
It will go to unbelieving Jews to persuade them that Jesus is the Christ, so the Father can restore Israel to its lands and fulfill his covenant.

It is also meant for the descendants of the Nephites and Lamanites to believe the gospel when it comes to them from the Gentiles. Mormon foresees them scattered and fallen into great spiritual degradation because of unbelief and idolatry.

f.w: dark, a filthy, and a loathsome people
f.g: Mormon’s description of spiritual and cultural decline; the Book of Mormon teaches that God invites all, “black and white,” to come to him.

chapters.n: The Spirit has already stopped striving with their fathers. Without Christ and God in the world, they are driven about like chaff in the wind.

f.g: The light husks blown away when grain is winnowed.

chapters.n: They were once a delightful people with Christ as their shepherd, led by God the Father himself.
Now Satan drives them about like chaff, or like a ship tossed on waves with no sail, anchor, or rudder. It is a vivid picture of life without God’s direction.
The blessings they could have had in the land are reserved for the Gentiles who will possess it.
Lehi’s descendants will be driven and scattered by the Gentiles; then the Lord will remember his covenant with Abraham and all Israel.

f.w: the covenant which he made unto Abraham

chapters.n: God will also remember the prayers of righteous people who prayed for these descendants — including Nephi, Enos, and Mormon himself.
Then Mormon turns to the Gentiles: how will you stand before God’s power unless you repent?
Don’t you know you’re in God’s hands, and he can roll up the earth like a scroll at his command?
So repent and humble yourselves, or God’s justice may come against you, and a remnant of Jacob may go among you like a lion with no one to rescue you.
Mormon now finishes his account of his people’s destruction. The Nephites march ahead of the advancing Lamanites.
Mormon writes to the Lamanite king asking permission to gather his people at the land and hill of Cumorah for a final battle.

f.g: Called Ramah by the Jaredites, where they too were destroyed.

chapters.n: Surprisingly, the Lamanite king agrees. Even in war, there are moments of formal courtesy.
The Nephites camp around the hill Cumorah, in a land of many rivers and springs, hoping the terrain will give them an advantage.
By 384 years after Christ, all the remaining Nephites are gathered at Cumorah.

Now old, Mormon knows this is the end. Commanded not to let the sacred records fall to the Lamanites, he hides them all in the hill Cumorah — except the abridgment on “these few plates,” which he gives to his son Moroni. These are the plates later given to Joseph Smith.

f.w: save it were these few plates which I gave unto my son Moroni
f.r: Mormon 8:1-5; Words of Mormon 1:1-2; Joseph Smith—History 1:51-52

chapters.n: The Nephites, with their families, watch the Lamanite armies approach, filled with the awful fear of death that grips the wicked.
The battle begins, and every Nephite is terrified by the enemy’s overwhelming numbers.
The Lamanites fall on them with swords, bows, arrows, axes, and every kind of weapon.
Mormon’s ten thousand are cut down, and he falls wounded among them. The Lamanites pass by without killing him.
Only 24 Nephites survive, including Moroni. The next day, from the top of Cumorah, they see the bodies of Mormon’s ten thousand.
They also see the fallen ten thousand led by Moroni.
Gidgiddonah and his ten thousand have fallen.
Mormon lists commander after commander who fell with ten thousand each. The roll call of names makes the scale of loss personal.

f.g: Not the earlier captain of the same name; names were reused across generations.

chapters.n: Ten more commanders fall with their armies — roughly 230,000 dead in all. Only the 24, some who escaped south, and some deserters remain. The bodies are left unburied to decay.
Mormon’s soul is torn with anguish over his slain people, and he cries out.
“O ye fair ones” — how could you leave the Lord’s ways and reject Jesus, who stood with open arms to receive you? It is one of the most heartbreaking laments in scripture.

f.w: stood with open arms to receive you

chapters.n: Had they not rejected him, they would not have fallen. Mormon mourns their loss.
He names them tenderly — sons and daughters, fathers and mothers, husbands and wives — and asks how they could have fallen.

f.w: how is it that ye could have fallen
f.g: Echoes David’s lament, “How are the mighty fallen!”

chapters.n: They are gone, and his grief cannot bring them back.
Soon their decaying bodies will be resurrected and made incorruptible, and they will stand before Christ’s judgment seat; the righteous among them will be blessed with their fathers.
If only they had repented before this! But they are gone, and the Eternal Father knows their state and will deal with them in justice and mercy. Mormon leaves them in God’s hands.

f.w: according to his justice and mercy

chapters.n: Mormon’s final words are addressed to the surviving descendants of his enemies — the remnant of Lehi in the last days. He hopes God will bring them his words so they can know their ancestors’ story.
His first message: know that you belong to the house of Israel. Identity comes first — they are covenant children.

f.w: ye are of the house of Israel

chapters.n: You must repent, or you cannot be saved. No one is exempt from this requirement.
Lay down your weapons, stop delighting in bloodshed, and don’t take them up again unless God commands. It is a plea born from Mormon’s lifetime of war.

f.w: lay down your weapons of war

chapters.n: Learn about your fathers, repent, and believe that Jesus is the Son of God — slain by the Jews and raised by the Father’s power, triumphing over the grave and removing death’s sting.

f.w: the sting of death swallowed up

chapters.n: Christ brings about the resurrection of the dead, so everyone will be raised to stand before his judgment seat.
Christ has redeemed the world. Those found guiltless at judgment will live in God’s presence, singing endless praises to the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost — one God — in never-ending happiness.

f.g: One in purpose and unity, as Latter-day Saints understand the Godhead.

chapters.n: So repent, be baptized in Jesus’ name, and hold fast to his gospel, found both in this record and in the Bible — the record from the Jews that comes to them through the Gentiles.

f.w: the record which shall come unto the Gentiles from the Jews

chapters.n: The Book of Mormon was written so they will believe the Bible; and believing the Bible, they will believe this too. The two records support each other.

f.w: if ye believe that ye will believe this also

chapters.n: They will know they are a remnant of Jacob, counted among the people of the first covenant. If they believe in Christ and are baptized by water, then by fire and the Holy Ghost, following the Savior’s example, all will be well at judgment. Mormon ends with “Amen.”

f.w: first with water, then with fire and with the Holy Ghost
following the example of our Savior

chapters.n: Moroni, Mormon’s son, takes over and finishes his father’s record. He has only a few things to write, as his father instructed.

f.g: The same Moroni who appeared to Joseph Smith as an angel in 1823.

chapters.n: After Cumorah, the Nephites who escaped south are hunted down by the Lamanites until all are destroyed.
Mormon is killed too. Moroni is left alone to write the sad story, fulfilling his father’s command, not knowing if he will be killed.
He will write and bury the records; where he goes afterward doesn’t matter. His only mission is preserving the record.

f.w: hide up the records in the earth

chapters.n: Moroni would add more but has no room on the plates and no ore to make more. His father and all his relatives are dead; he has no friends and nowhere to go. It is one of the loneliest verses in scripture.

f.g: No raw metal to make more plates.

chapters.n: Four hundred years have passed since Christ’s coming — fulfilling the prophecy of the Nephites’ end.
The Lamanites hunted the Nephites city by city until none remained. Their fall was great and marvelous.
Moroni recognizes the Lord’s hand in this judgment. Meanwhile the Lamanites fight among themselves; the land is an endless cycle of murder, and no one knows when the war will end.
He says no more about them, since only Lamanites and robbers remain in the land.
Only the Three Nephites knew the true God, but the Lord removed them because of extreme wickedness; no one knows whether they are still in the land.

f.w: the disciples of Jesus, who did tarry

chapters.n: Yet Moroni and his father have seen them, and they ministered to them.
Whoever receives this record without condemning its imperfections will learn greater things. Moroni wishes he could reveal everything.

f.g: Human weaknesses in the writing, not errors in doctrine.

chapters.n: Moroni closes his comments about his people, identifying himself as Mormon’s son and a descendant of Nephi.
He is the one who hides the record. The plates have no worth for profit — no one may use them for gain — but the record is of great worth, and God will bless whoever brings it to light.
Only one empowered by God can bring it forth, and it must be done with an eye single to God’s glory and the welfare of scattered Israel.

f.w: an eye single to his glory

chapters.n: Blessed is the one who brings it to light. It will come out of the earth and shine forth from darkness by God’s power — a prophecy of the Book of Mormon’s coming forth.
If there are faults, they are human faults. Those who condemn the record should beware of the danger of hell fire.

f.g: The Book of Mormon title page also asks readers not to blame God for human mistakes.

chapters.n: Whoever demands to see the plates under threat should be careful, lest he demand what the Lord has forbidden.
Those who judge rashly will be judged rashly. As people treat others, they will be paid back; those who strike will be struck by the Lord.
Scripture says man should neither strike nor judge; judgment and vengeance belong to the Lord.

f.w: vengeance is mine also, and I will repay

chapters.n: Those who rage against God’s work and covenant people, saying they will destroy his work and the Lord won’t remember Israel, are in danger of being cut down and burned.
God’s eternal purposes will roll on until every promise is fulfilled. Nothing can stop his work.

f.w: the eternal purposes of the Lord shall roll on

chapters.n: Search Isaiah’s prophecies. The saints who once lived here will cry to the Lord “from the dust” — through this buried record — and God will remember his covenant with them.
God knows their prayers were for their brethren, and knows their faith: by his name they moved mountains, shook the earth, toppled prisons, and survived furnaces, beasts, and serpents.
They also prayed for the one the Lord would allow to bring these records forth — prayers for Joseph Smith, centuries before his birth.

f.w: him that the Lord should suffer to bring these things forth

chapters.n: No one should say the records will never come; they surely will, by the Lord’s hand. They will appear when people say miracles have ended, like a voice from the dead.

f.w: as if one should speak from the dead

chapters.n: Here begins a prophetic description of our day: the blood of saints will cry to the Lord because of secret combinations and works of darkness.
God’s power will be denied, churches will become corrupt and proud, and leaders and teachers will rise in pride, even envying their own members.
People will hear of fires, storms, and smoke in foreign lands — news of disasters reaching around the world.
There will be wars, rumors of wars, and earthquakes in various places — signs Jesus himself listed.
Great moral pollution will cover the earth, and many will teach that sin doesn’t matter because the Lord will save them anyway. Woe to such people, trapped in bitterness and sin.

f.w: it mattereth not, for the Lord will uphold such

chapters.n: Churches will arise that offer forgiveness of sins for money.

f.w: for your money you shall be forgiven

chapters.n: Moroni rebukes those who build churches for profit and twist God’s word, bringing condemnation on themselves. Look to God’s revelations, for all these things will be fulfilled.

f.w: transfigured the holy word of God

chapters.n: The Lord has shown Moroni great things about the time when this record comes forth.
Moroni speaks as if we were present, because Jesus Christ has shown us to him and he knows what we do. He is writing directly to modern readers.

f.w: Jesus Christ hath shown you unto me

chapters.n: He sees that we walk in pride — fine clothes, envy, strife, malice, persecution — and that every church has become polluted by pride, except a few people.
We love money, possessions, fine clothes, and decorated churches more than the poor, needy, sick, and afflicted. A sharp warning against materialism.

f.w: more than ye love the poor and the needy

chapters.n: Moroni calls out hypocrites and teachers who sell themselves for perishable things. Why be ashamed of Christ’s name? Why trade endless happiness for the world’s praise?

f.w: ashamed to take upon you the name of Christ

chapters.n: Why decorate yourselves with lifeless things while ignoring the hungry, needy, naked, sick, and afflicted who pass by?
Why build secret evils for profit, making widows and orphans mourn and the blood of murdered men cry from the ground for justice?

f.w: cry unto the Lord from the ground

chapters.n: The sword of vengeance hangs over such people. God will soon avenge the saints’ blood, for he will no longer allow their cries to go unanswered.
Moroni now addresses those who do not believe in Christ. This chapter is his powerful testimony to skeptics of every age.
He asks: when the Lord comes and the earth is rolled up and the elements melt, when you stand before the Lamb of God — will you still say there is no God?

f.g: The time when God comes to judge or bless.

f.w: the elements shall melt with fervent heat

chapters.n: Will you still deny Christ then? Could you even bear to look at him? Do you think you could be happy living with a holy Being while tormented by awareness of having broken his laws?
Moroni says such a person would be more miserable living with a holy God than with the damned in hell. Heaven would not feel like heaven to an unrepentant heart.

f.w: more miserable to dwell with a holy and just God

chapters.n: Seeing your own spiritual nakedness beside God’s glory and Christ’s holiness would be like an unquenchable fire. The “fire” is in part the burning awareness of guilt.

f.g: Being fully exposed, with nothing hidden.

chapters.n: So turn to the Lord now, cry mightily to the Father in Jesus’ name, and perhaps you can be found spotless, pure, and white, cleansed by the Lamb’s blood at the last day.

f.w: cleansed by the blood of the Lamb

chapters.n: Next Moroni speaks to those who say revelation, prophecy, spiritual gifts, healing, and tongues have ceased.
Whoever denies these things doesn’t know the gospel — he either hasn’t read the scriptures or doesn’t understand them.

f.w: knoweth not the gospel of Christ

chapters.n: Scripture teaches that God is the same yesterday, today, and forever, with no variation or shadow of change.

f.w: the same yesterday, today, and forever
no variableness neither shadow of changing

chapters.n: If you imagine a God who changes, you have invented a god who is not a God of miracles. The real God does not change his nature.

f.g: Made up in your own minds.

chapters.n: Moroni will show them the God of miracles: the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who created the heavens, the earth, and everything in them.

f.w: the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob

chapters.n: God created Adam; through Adam came the Fall; because of the Fall came Jesus Christ, “the Father and the Son”; and through Christ came redemption. It is the plan of salvation in one verse.

f.w: by Adam came the fall of man

f.g: Christ is called Father as Creator and as the one who gives us new birth, and Son because of his mortal body.

chapters.n: Through redemption all people return to God’s presence. Christ’s death brings resurrection, waking all from the “endless sleep” when the trumpet sounds; all will stand at his judgment bar, freed from physical death.

f.g: His judgment seat, like a court.

chapters.n: Then comes judgment, and people remain what they have become: the filthy stay filthy, the righteous stay righteous, the happy stay happy.

f.w: he that is filthy shall be filthy still

chapters.n: To those who believe in a God who cannot do miracles: has the end come yet? No — so God has not stopped being a God of miracles.
Aren’t God’s works marvelous to us? Who can fully understand them?
Wasn’t creation itself a miracle — heaven and earth by his word, man from the dust, and miracles by his power?

f.w: man was created of the dust of the earth

chapters.n: Who can deny that Jesus and his apostles worked mighty miracles?

f.w: wrought by the hands of the apostles

chapters.n: If God worked miracles then, why would he stop and still be unchangeable? He does not change — if he did, he would not be God — so he remains a God of miracles.
The reason miracles stop is unbelief: people dwindle in disbelief, leave the right way, and don’t know the God they should trust. Miracles follow faith; they don’t create it.

f.w: because that they dwindle in unbelief

chapters.n: Whoever believes in Christ without doubting will receive what he asks the Father in Christ’s name — a promise to the whole earth.
Jesus said to his disciples, including the three who would remain, in the multitude’s hearing: go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature.

f.w: Go ye into all the world

chapters.n: Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; whoever does not believe will be condemned.

f.w: he that believeth and is baptized shall be saved

chapters.n: Signs will follow believers: casting out devils, new tongues, protection from serpents and poison, and healing the sick by laying on of hands.

f.w: these signs shall follow them that believe

chapters.n: Whoever believes in Christ’s name without doubting will see Christ confirm all his words, everywhere on earth.
Who can fight God’s work, deny his words, or despise his children? Those who scorn his works will wonder and perish.

Don’t scorn or merely marvel — listen, ask the Father in Jesus’ name for what you need, don’t doubt, come to the Lord with all your heart as in ancient times, and work out your salvation with fear and trembling.

f.w: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling

chapters.n: Use this probationary life wisely: put away impurity, don’t ask for things just to satisfy your appetites, and ask with unshakable resolve to resist temptation and serve the living God.
Don’t be baptized or take the sacrament unworthily; do everything worthily in Christ’s name. Endure to the end and you will never be cast out.

f.w: partake not of the sacrament of Christ unworthily

chapters.n: Moroni speaks as if from the dead, knowing his words will reach us.

f.w: as though I spake from the dead

chapters.n: Don’t condemn him, his father, or earlier writers for their imperfections; thank God for revealing them so you can be wiser than they were.
The record was written in “reformed Egyptian,” a script modified over time by the Nephites to suit their language.

f.g: A modified Egyptian script; it took less space than Hebrew.

chapters.n: With larger plates they would have written in Hebrew, which they had also altered; then the record would have no imperfection. Writing space shaped their choices.

f.w: the Hebrew hath been altered by us also
f.g: Their language had changed over a thousand years.

chapters.n: The Lord knows what they wrote, and since no one else knows their language, he prepared a means of interpretation — the interpreters later used by Joseph Smith.
They write so as to rid their garments of their brethren’s blood — fulfilling their duty to warn, so they are not responsible for others’ sins.

f.w: rid our garments of the blood

chapters.n: The desire that their brethren be restored to knowledge of Christ matches the prayers of all the saints who lived in this land.

f.w: according to the prayers of all the saints

chapters.n: Moroni prays that Christ will answer those prayers according to their faith, that the Father will remember his covenant with Israel, and that he will bless them forever through faith in Jesus. Amen.
